title: Cohort-aware KV compacting: FP8/INT8/INT4 quality vs GPU-memory trade study
creator: Aisha Kumar
description:
Goal: Determine operational sweet spots for KV cache quantization and compacting in the continuous batching path. We want to reclaim GPU memory for higher concurrency without creating unacceptable quality regressions or tail-latency spikes. This investigation measures FP8, INT8, and INT4 encodings applied to hot and cold KV cohorts with two compacting policies (age-based eviction vs. tiered re-quantization), plus a sliding-window re-quantization fallback for degraded outputs.

Hypotheses: 1) FP8 applied universally to recent KV entries will offer ~25-35% memory reduction with negligible quality impact. 2) INT8 can be used aggressively for older/cohorted entries to get additional memory savings while keeping on-path prefix fidelity high. 3) INT4 gives large memory wins but needs cohort-aware safeguards (e.g., keep last N tokens in FP16/FP32 and only quantize older tokens) to avoid hallucination spikes.

Scope: Live-traffic shadow testing + synthetic eval set composed of: long-context summarization (50k tokens window), multi-turn dialogue, and retrieval-augmented generation prompts with entity resolution checks. Metrics: end-to-end latency P50/P95, tokens/sec throughput, GPU memory footprint, token-level cross-entropy delta vs baseline, exact-match on entity spans, and qualitative hallucination incidents per 10k responses.
experiment_matrix: Baseline: FP16 KV (no compaction), continuous batching=adaptive, batch_size cap=64
Variant A: FP8 on all KV entries + age-eviction at 60s
Variant B: FP8 recent (last 1024 tokens), INT8 for entries 1025-8192, age-eviction at 120s
Variant C: Tiered: keep last 2048 tokens FP16, next 8192 tokens INT8, rest INT4 + sliding-window re-quantize on high perplexity segments
Variant D: Aggressive INT4 for cold cohorts + canary rollback to INT8 per-request when token-logprob delta > threshold
Fallback: per-request dynamic re-quantize: if generation perplexity increases > 5% vs cached baseline for first 50 tokens, re-fetch last N=128 KV entries in FP16 and re-generate
runs: Shadow run on live traffic subset (5% of production) for 48 hours
Controlled sweep on synthetic eval (10k prompts per workload type) with 3 seeds
Microbench on dedicated dev-GPU farm for memory/save-throughput profiling (A100/80GB)
results_summary: Baseline memory usage (FP16 KV): 28.5 GB per model shard @ typical 8k-context workload
Variant A (FP8-all): memory 19.8 GB (-30.5%), throughput +14% P50, P95 latency unchanged, quality: token-level cross-entropy delta +0.02 nats, entity EM -0.3%

Variant B (FP8 recent + INT8 mid): memory 16.4 GB (-42.5%), throughput +28% P50, P95 latency +3% (due to on-path dequant steps), quality: cross-entropy delta +0.06 nats, entity EM -0.9%, rare hallucination incidents +0.4/10k

Variant C (tiered w/INT4 cold): memory 10.2 GB (-64.2%), throughput +58% P50 but P95 tail increased by 18% in long-context RAG cases where re-quantization kicked in, quality: cross-entropy delta +0.42 nats, entity EM -3.1%, hallucination incidents +6.8/10k in long-context summarization workload

Variant D (aggressive INT4 + per-request rollback): similar memory to Variant C but live shadow showed frequent rollbacks on 6% of requests; effective average latency increased and throughput dropped back to ~+25% over baseline, quality restored after rollback but rollback churn creates extra CPU overhead
Fallback effectiveness: sliding-window re-quantize prevented 74% of hallucination incidents in Variant C at the cost of ~12% extra P95 latency for those requests.
analysis_and_tradeoffs: FP8-all (Variant A) appears to be low-risk and gives consistent memory and throughput wins with minimal quality delta — recommended as default compaction layer for recent KV entries.

INT8 mid-tier (Variant B) is attractive for predictable capacity because memory savings are large and average latency gain is meaningful, but we must account for a small increase in tail latency due to dequant overhead and occasional decreased entity fidelity. Best applied to cohorts identified as low-entity-cohesion (e.g., system prompts, static embeddings).

"INT4 for cold cohorts" (Variant C) delivers the largest memory reclaim but introduces non-trivial quality regressions on long-context and RAG workloads. The sliding-window re-quantize fallback mitigates but does not fully eliminate regressions; rollout only for non-critical tenants or behind an opt-in flag and monitored heavily.
Operational costs: rollback/rollback-churn increases CPU and memory pressure in the control plane. Canarying with per-tenant thresholds and telemetry is required before wide rollout.
decisions_and_actions: Ship FP8-for-recent-kv as experiment flag default: runtime-2.6:kv.fp8_recent=true (engineering rollout target: next two sprints)
Implement cohort classifier (heuristic + ML) to label KV entries as hot/retrieval/system so INT8 can be applied safely to low-risk cohorts — tracked in ENG-176900
Gate INT4 behind: tenant opt-in + canary only; create rollback circuit that samples re-quantization hits and triggers auto-disable for tenant if hallucination rate > 2/10k over 1h
Add new telemetry: token_logprob_delta, cohort_label, re-quant_count, rollback_count, hallucination_incident_id — surface in Console per-route dashboard
Follow-up experiment: test per-layer mixed precision (e.g., keep attention-kv in FP16 while MLP-kv in INT8) — estimate tracked in ENG-175999
open_questions: What are tenant-level thresholds we should expose for safe INT4 opt-in? (suggested starting point: 0.5% allowed EM regression)
How to cost-account for rollback churn (CPU and network) in pricing model for Dedicated customers?
Can we train a lightweight quality predictor that can trigger re-quantize before user-visible regression occurs?
